PART FIVE
Loss & Grief
CHAPTER 44
When Someone You Love Dies
People may be asking you to make decisions while you are still
trying to understand that the person has died. There are calls to
answer and arrangements to consider. Then a quiet moment
arrives, and the fact of their absence becomes difficult to take in
again.
Perhaps the death happened some time ago. The funeral is over,
other people have resumed their routines, and you are
discovering what an ordinary week now requires. The person is
missing from parts of the day no ceremony could have prepared
you for.
Grief may include tears, anger, or a numbness that surprises
you. A moment of laughter may come too. None of these, taken
alone, can measure the love between you. You can begin with
what is happening today, even if it differs from what you
expected to feel.
Jesus comes to a grieving household
John 11:17–44
When Jesus reached Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb for
four days. Many people had come to console his sisters, Martha

219
and Mary. Martha went out to meet Jesus and told Him that if
He had been there, her brother would not have died.
Jesus spoke with her about resurrection. Martha believed that
Lazarus would rise at the last day. Jesus declared that He
Himself was the resurrection and the life, and asked about her
faith. Later, Mary came to Him with the same words about her
brother's death. Seeing her and the people with her weeping,
Jesus was deeply moved and troubled.
Jesus wept.
John 11:35, Berean Standard Bible
He went to the tomb and called Lazarus out. The man who had
died came out still wrapped in burial cloths, and Jesus told the
people to unbind him.
The account holds Jesus' authority over death together with His
tears beside the bereaved. His conversation about resurrection
did not make the sisters' grief unworthy of His attention. Their
questions were spoken in His presence.
Lazarus' return was a sign of Jesus' authority over death.
Christian hope rests on Jesus Himself, whose death and
resurrection are the foundation of the promise Christians
receive. It does not depend on this death being reversed now or
on your finding enough faith to remove the ache.
If you have a question that sounds more like Martha's protest
than a settled prayer, bring it to Him. "Why were You not
there?" may be difficult to say. The Gospel gives us a
conversation in which words like those are heard.

220
Hope while someone is still missing
Paul wrote to Christians concerned about members of their
community who had died. In 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18, he
addresses their grief by speaking about Jesus' return and the
resurrection of those who belong to Him. He asks them to
encourage one another with that hope.
He does not tell the church to stop grieving. Their hope concerns
being with the Lord, including those who have died in Christ.
You may have questions about the faith of the person you lost.
Speak about those questions with someone who will treat them
carefully. You do not need to invent certainty about another
person's relationship with God to make other people
comfortable. You can entrust what you do not know to His
mercy and judgment.
Revelation 21:1–5 looks toward God's dwelling with His people,
the wiping away of tears, and the end of death and mourning.
That promised future gives a grieving Christian something to
hope for while the present remains painful.
What would help with this day?
Choose one need close enough to act on. You might need food
brought into the house, someone to sit with you, or help making
a call you have postponed. Give a trusted person a request they
can understand: "Could you come with me to this appointment?"
or "Can we eat together tonight?"
Where arrangements and paperwork are involved, ask someone
reliable to help keep track of what needs attention. Some
matters have deadlines; others can wait. You can ask the
relevant professional which is which, rather than assuming
every request needs an immediate answer.
There may be decisions about belongings that no one needs you
to make today. Keep what helps, put something aside if seeing it

221
is too difficult, and allow decisions to be revisited. There is no
object you must keep or remove in order to prove your love.
Grief can affect sleep and concentration. Be gentle about what
you expect from yourself, and seek help if you are struggling to
manage daily life. A bereavement counselor or support group
can offer a place to speak about the loss. If grief brings thoughts
of ending your own life, seek crisis support immediately; if you
may act on those thoughts, contact local emergency services.
If someone you care about is bereaved
Offer a specific kindness and give them room to decline. A meal
on Thursday or help with an errand is easier to consider than an
unlimited offer they must work out how to use.
Ask whether they would like to talk about the person who died.
Use the person's name if that is welcome, and share a memory
you actually have. Listen if their experience differs from the
relationship you knew. Avoid explaining what God intended by
the death or asking them to reassure you that they are coping.
Keep in touch beyond the first days. When you arrange a visit,
let them know that they do not have to entertain you or produce
a new account of how they are doing.
A prayer
Jesus, You stood with people who wept for someone they loved. Be
with me in the absence I am learning to live with. Receive the
questions I cannot settle. Help me accept the care I need and face the
tasks that cannot wait. Hold me in the hope of Your risen life when
my own words are few. In Your name, amen.
Pause and reflect
What about this loss do you most need to say to God today?

222
Which task or ordinary need could someone help you with now?
For further reading: John 11:17–44; Psalm 6:6–9; Matthew 5:4; 1 Thessalonians
4:13–18; Revelation 21:1–5.

• When an Anniversary Brings Grief Back (p. 247), for dates and occasions that bring
the absence close again.
